sentences.text: Andalgalornis was a flightless predatory bird belonging to the extinct family Phorusrhacidae, commonly known as terror birds, that lived in Argentina.
The only known species of the genus Andalgalornis is A. steulleti.
This animal stood approximately 1.4 meters tall and weighed about 40 kilograms.
Although it resembled the larger Phorusrhacos, Andalgalornis was more elegant, smaller, and possessed the most massive beak relative to its body size among all phorusrhacids.
Fossil evidence suggests it preyed on small rodent-like mammals such as Paedotherium.
Fossils of Andalgalornis include an incomplete skeleton and isolated bones found in the Entre Ríos and Catamarca Provinces of Argentina.
The fossils were recovered in April 1926 by a US paleontological expedition led by geologist Germán Young and collector Rudolf Stahlecker, assisted by local guides Juan and Felipe Méndez.
Research suggests Andalgalornis had a skull adapted for rigidity, showing high stress under sideways loads but low stress when force was applied vertically or during pullback simulations.
CT scans suggest Andalgalornis had a beak that was strong vertically but relatively weak laterally.
Researchers suggest the strong vertical beak of Andalgalornis may have allowed it to quickly strike prey using a repetitive attack-and-retreat hunting strategy.
Researchers suggest Andalgalornis likely fed on small prey or used an attack-and-retreat strategy with repetitive strikes against larger prey rather than subduing them directly.
A 2012 study found that the neck of Andalgalornis was divided into three sections and adapted for carrying a large head and rising after a downward strike.
A study of the neck vertebrae indicated they were structurally adapted for striking.
Andalgalornis is classified in the order Cariamiformes and family Phorusrhacidae, with the genus authority cited as Patterson & Kraglievich, 1960.
Andalgalornis has several synonyms, including Phororhacos steulleti, Phororhacos deautieri, Andalgalornis ferox, and Phorohacos deautieri.
Andalgalornis fossils were discovered in the Late Miocene Ituzaingó Formation within the Paraná Basin.
Andalgalornis fossils date from 7 to 5 million years ago and were found in the Andalhuala Formation in the Santa María Valley of Catamarca Province, Argentina.
The time range for the genus Andalgalornis is estimated from 8 to 5 million years ago.
